name: Carla Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that's fine. I like that it's confidential, because some of what I think I wouldn't say in the site canteen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do second fix, which is the carpentry after the plasterers leave: doors, skirting boards, stairs, kitchen units. I'm on a new-build estate called Orchard Fields for Brightstone Homes, and I get paid per house, not per hour. A good day I hang twelve doors and get the skirting round two floors. I love seeing a house go from bare walls to looking like someone could live there, but my knees and wrists are already complaining at 27.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's money like at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. The plot rate has been cut once in two years, and rent went up in the spring. I live with my boyfriend Theo, who drives a city bus, and between us we save almost nothing. I do the odd weekend job fitting wardrobes for people, and I've started using a chat AI to help me write the quotes so they sound professional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So basically today. I'm using AI to write a quote now and then and that's as far as it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was always oversold. I'd probably joke in the canteen that the robots still can't hang a door straight. Online I'd say the real fight is about pay, not tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is fine for my job, but it doesn't fix my money. Orchard Fields has about three years of houses left, so the work's there, but the plot rate is low and rent keeps going up. I'm okay, not comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my plots and push the weekend wardrobe jobs a bit harder, maybe two a month instead of one. I'd keep using the AI for quotes because it saves me an evening each time. And I'd go to the women in trades meetups, because that's where I hear about better-paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the job, a bit tired about the money. It's a background hum, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plot rate was cut once. What happened when it was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brightstone said material prices had gone up and dropped the rate for a door by a fifth. Three of us complained and they said take it or leave it. I took the pay cut, because where else am I going? The next big building site is an hour and a half away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a weekend job paid well, would you think of going on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a few years, not now. I've got less than a month's rent saved and I'd need a van. Theo would worry, and honestly so would I.

say: AI was always **oversold**, and robots still can't **hang a door** straight.
The real fight on site is about **pay**, not technology.
think: Her **job** is safe, with about **three years** of houses left at Orchard Fields.
A low **plot rate** and rising rent mean she is okay, not comfortable.
do: Take on **two weekend jobs** a month fitting wardrobes instead of one.
Keep using a chat AI to write **quotes**, saving an evening each time.
Attend **women in trades** meetups to hear about better-paid work.
feel: Fairly **calm** about the job, a bit **tired** about money.
S0.quote: I took the pay cut, because where else am I going? The next big building site is an hour and a half away.
fieldNote: Her **work looks secure** for three years, but thin savings keep money on her mind, so **uneasy**.
Already uses **AI for quotes**, a practical steady adopter.
The **plot rate cut** shows how little bargaining power few local jobs leave her.

steps.text: Fit two weekend wardrobes a month instead of one
Keep using a chat AI to write weekend job quotes
Keep hanging doors per plot at Orchard Fields

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one hits the office at Brightstone first, I think. The people who order the materials and plan which plot gets done when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a say in how this gets brought in, and we need the union in on it early. On site I'd tell people our hands are safe for now, but the people above us will change. I'd share stuff about retraining support online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Brightstone will use the software to squeeze us harder. If a computer plans every plot to the hour, the bosses will know exactly how fast I am and set the rate to the fastest person. And Theo's bus company already talks about AI timetables, so his shifts could change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly this year instead of just meaning to. I'd learn whatever planning app Brightstone brings in so I'm not the one who looks slow. And I'd start putting fifty a month into savings even if it means fewer nights out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not panicking, but I'd be watching every email from the site office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd set the rate to the fastest person. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of, yes. Last year they timed a young guy called Marek on the stair fits and then everyone's stair rate dropped. He was fast but he was also cutting corners on the fixings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if Theo's shifts changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose his overtime, which is what pays for the car. We'd probably sell the car and I'd get a lift to site with my foreman Jo. It's annoying but we'd manage.

say: Workers need a **say** in how AI is brought in, with the **union** involved early.
Site hands are safe **for now**, but the jobs above them will change.
think: Planning software could let Brightstone set **plot rates** to the fastest worker.
Theo's **bus shifts** could change under AI timetables, hitting household income.
do: Learn Brightstone's new **planning app** quickly so she doesn't look slow.
Save **fifty a month** by cutting nights out.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, watching every site office email.
S1.quote: If a computer plans every plot to the hour, the bosses will know exactly how fast I am and set the rate to the fastest person.
fieldNote: Sees AI planning as a tool for **squeezing piece rates**, not cutting jobs outright.
Household exposure via Theo's **overtime** makes this more than unease.
Steady adopter: would **learn the app** defensively, not eagerly.

steps.text: Join the construction union at Orchard Fields this year
Learn Brightstone's plot planning app in the first month
Save fifty a month by cutting nights out
Sell the car if Theo loses overtime and share lifts to site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. So the planning and ordering is gone by 2028, and then by 2031 a robot can hang a door as well as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a government plan now, a proper one, like paying people while they retrain and taxing the firms that own the robots. I'd go on marches for that. I'd tell people on site it's not their fault and not to blame each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared for both of us. My boyfriend Theo drives a bus, and a robot driver is basically what this card describes, so his job and mine could both go around 2031. We have nothing saved, and I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd work every plot I can get, because builders would rush to finish houses before prices change. I'd save every spare penny, maybe two hundred a month by moving into a cheaper flat. And I'd look hard at moving into something like building inspection or snagging for home buyers, where people still want a person to sign it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and kind of angry that it'd be so fast nobody could plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned building inspection. Isn't that partly thinking work that AI would take in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, you're right, the report writing would go first. I suppose I'm hoping people still want a human to walk round and put their hand on the wall. I don't really know, it's more a hope than a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Theo talk about the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether to move back in with my mum to save rent. Neither of us would want that. But with both jobs at risk, we'd have to talk about it.

say: The **government** needs a plan now: pay people to retrain and **tax robot owners**.
Site workers shouldn't **blame each other** for what's happening.
think: Her job and Theo's **bus job** could both go around **2031**.
With **nothing saved**, she'd be 32 facing that loss.
do: Work every **plot** possible during the rush before robots arrive.
Move to a **cheaper flat** to save about two hundred a month.
Look into **snagging and inspection** work for home buyers.
feel: **Frightened**, and **angry** that it's too fast to plan for.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Theo drives a bus, and a robot driver is basically what this card describes, so his job and mine could both go around 2031.
fieldNote: Two-earner exposure: her **carpentry** and Theo's **bus driving** both fall to robots by 2031.
Admits her **inspection** idea is a hope more than a plan.
Considers moving in with her **mum**, a sign of how thin the cushion is.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper flat and save two hundred a month
Look into snagging inspection work for new home buyers
March for paid retraining and a tax on robot owners
Talk with Theo about moving in with her mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So 2031 for the AI and 2034 for the robots. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions and government to plan, while there's time. I'd be pushing that in the union branch and online. I'd also say to younger people on site, start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for me to get one extra skill but not enough to save much. Brightstone would still need hands till 2034, so the first few years would look normal. The danger is that normal makes us lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening course in site supervision, because overseeing robots on site might be a real job for a while. I'd keep the weekend wardrobe work going and put that money straight into savings. And I'd ask the union rep to get Brightstone to pay for some of the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but more in control. I could actually do something with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said overseeing robots might be a job for a while. How long do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't know, maybe a few years, until they don't need watching either. But a few years of better pay overseeing robots could be the difference between having savings and not. That's worth it to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to do the evening course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my Thursday football and some of the weekend jobs. Theo would have to cook more. He's actually a better cook than me, so that's fine.

say: Unions and government should **plan now**, while there's **time**.
Younger site workers should **start learning** new skills now.
think: Five years is enough for **one new skill** but not enough to **save** much.
The first years looking **normal** could make workers lazy about preparing.
do: Start an evening course in **site supervision** in the first year.
Put **weekend job** money straight into savings.
Ask the union rep to get Brightstone to **fund training**.
feel: **Nervous** but more **in control** with five years.
S3.quote: A few years of better pay overseeing robots could be the difference between having savings and not.
fieldNote: The extra time turns fear into a **concrete plan**: supervision training.
Still **anxious**, since her trade and Theo's job still end by **2034**.
Willing to **give up football** and weekend jobs to study.

steps.text: Start an evening course in site supervision
Put weekend wardrobe money straight into savings
Ask the union rep to get Brightstone to fund courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the AI and robots in 2039. I'd be 40 by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly if anyone actually plans. I'd tell everyone at the union to push for retraining money now, not in year nine. And I'd talk about it openly at the women in trades group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one where I can see a path. Ten years of work, a supervision ticket, maybe a small business fitting kitchens until robots come, and some savings. But I still don't know what I'd do at 40 once robots can do it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the supervision course in the next year and maybe a kitchen design course later. I'd try to buy a van with Theo in about three years and do kitchens on my own. And I'd keep pushing in the union for proper training money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, actually, with a bit of worry at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why kitchens and not doors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people care about their kitchen and they want to talk to the person fitting it. Nobody chats to you about skirting boards. A kitchen job is a relationship, and that's harder to hand to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when 2039 comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't know. Maybe I'm running a few robots instead of fitting things myself. Or maybe I'm doing something completely different by then, and that's okay.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to do this fairly if anyone plans.
The union should push for **retraining money** now, not in year nine.
think: This is the one picture where she can **see a path**.
She still doesn't know what she'd do at **40** once robots do it all.
do: Take the **supervision course** in the next year.
Buy a **van** with Theo in about three years to fit kitchens solo.
Keep pushing the union for **training money**.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a bit of **worry** about the end point.
S4.quote: People care about their kitchen and they want to talk to the person fitting it. Nobody chats to you about skirting boards.
fieldNote: The decade gives her a **business idea**: fitting kitchens, where customers want a person.
Still **anxious** because savings are thin and the **end point** is unresolved.
Plans are paced and proven-first, true to a **steady** adopter.

steps.text: Take a site supervision course next year
Buy a van in three years and fit kitchens on her own
Push the union for training money now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Theo and I would both be out within a couple of years of each other. What would help is money while you retrain, so people like us don't have to choose between rent and a course. And a union that's actually at the table when firms bring robots in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in trades. We only just got here, and we're the newest and the least senior, so we'd be first out the door. Getting taken seriously on site took me years, and I'd hate to lose it all to a machine.

headlineQuote: Getting taken seriously on site took me years, and I'd hate to lose it all to a machine.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old second-fix carpenter**, paid per house on a new-build estate.
Her **plot rate** has been cut and she lives with Theo, a **bus driver**, with almost no savings.
She's a **steady adopter** who already uses AI for weekend quotes and joins the union when it counts.
She fears AI planning will **squeeze pay** first, then robots take both her job and Theo's.
With **ten years** she sees a path through supervision and fitting kitchens for customers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Theo could both lose their jobs around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** so she doesn't have to choose between rent and a course.
A **union** at the table when firms bring in robots.
